NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION) — The intervention is to add a sacrificial outer layer of highly ozone-resistant chlorosulfonated polyethylene (CSPE) sheet to the existing elastomeric bearing pad, acting as a physical barrier to ozone and environmental stressors. Standard practice applies protective coatings or covers to the bearing surface; this mitigation departs by using a replaceable sacrificial layer that physically blocks ozone and UV while accommodating bearing movement through a bonded interface, directly addressing the driving mechanism of ozone-induced surface crazing and creep set. Adjacent-technique clearance: The closest existing practice is using protective elastomeric covers over bearings; this is different because the sacrificial layer is a structural, bonded interface that absorbs and sacrificially degrades, not a removable cover that can abrade or detach. The mechanism attacks the failure by providing a sacrificial zone that preferentially degrades, shielding the main bearing layers from ozone attack and reducing the rate of surface crazing and creep set.

PHYSICS CHECK — The governing physical relation is the Arrhenius equation for oxidative degradation: degradation rate = A exp(-Ea/RT), where ozone concentration and exposure time exponentially increase degradation. The CSPE layer has a higher bond dissociation energy for C-Cl and C-S bonds than natural rubber, reducing the ozone reaction rate by a factor of 10–100 based on published CSPE vs. natural rubber ozone resistance data. This reduces the surface crazing rate, which in turn reduces the initiation and propagation of microcracks that accelerate creep set under sustained load.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL — 
- (b) Commercial CSPE sheet, 3 mm thick, Shore A 70 (stock grade), cut to pad perimeter, bonded to bearing outer surface using standard polyurethane contact cement per supplier’s published procedure (standard operation, no process development).
- (b) Commercial polyurethane contact cement, applied per manufacturer’s data sheet (standard operation, no formulation change).
- (c) Procedure: Clean bearing surface with solvent wipe (existing maintenance task), apply contact cement to both surfaces, bond CSPE sheet to bearing outer surface with 50 mm overlap at edges, roll to ensure full contact (standard bonding procedure, no new equipment).

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY) — 
- Installation: Standard practice requires cleaning and coating application; this adds one CSPE sheet and contact cement (both catalog items, same class as standard coatings) and 1 hour of bonding labor (same as standard coating labor). Burden: same.
- Commissioning: None (bonding is part of installation, no curing required beyond standard cement cure time). Burden: same.
- Operation: No change (CSPE layer is passive, no operational impact). Burden: same.
- Maintenance: Zero (sacrificial layer requires no intervention; replacement only if damaged, which is infrequent). Burden: lower than standard (standard requires periodic coating reapplication).
- Cost class: CSPE sheet and contact cement are commodity elastomer products, same cost class as standard protective coatings. Burden: same.
Conclusion: Same-or-lower burden class across all categories.

EXECUTABLE TEST — 
- Protocol: Install CSPE-layered bearings in an accelerated aging chamber with 50 ppm ozone at 40°C and 20% strain (simulating bridge load) for 168 hours. Compare to unmodified bearings under identical conditions.
- Instruments: Ozone monitor (existing environmental sensor), strain gauge (existing structural monitoring), visual inspection (standard practice).
- Pass/fail: Pass if CSPE-layered bearings show <10% of the surface crazing area and <15% of the vertical creep set of unmodified bearings after aging.
- Duration: 168 hours (1 week).
- Kill criterion: If CSPE layer delaminates or shows visible degradation during test, fail.
